sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
We only have a full year of history for a few Frankfurt garages, so there is no city trend yet; the figures below are for weekdays in August and September 2026.

Frankfurt has set out its aim of moving people out of cars explicitly. Its mobility masterplan, adopted in 2025, aims for 80% of trips on foot, by bike or public transport by 2035, up from 67%, with higher parking fees among its main measures [4]. The street came first: from 2019 the free spaces inside the Alleenring became paid [0], and resident permits rose almost fivefold in January 2024, from €50 to €240 for two years [3]. Closing the Mainkai riverside to cars was agreed in stages; in summer 2023 it was shut for ten weeks and then reopened [1][2]. In return the city plans about 3,000 new park-and-ride spaces on the edge, without a timetable [5]. The chamber of commerce counts 43% of city-centre visitors from outside Frankfurt, most of them by car [11].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
The city's own garage company PBG has been modernising rather than expanding: plate-recognition entry in twelve garages [9] and, with Mainova, hundreds of charge points across eleven public garages from 2023 [6][7]. The wider city counted over 2,100 public charge points by 2026 [8].

The weak spot is information. The municipal parking guidance system, which tells drivers where spaces are free, was cut off in 2022 over IT security and switched off; a replacement was not expected to start construction before mid-2026 [10]. Large shopping centres on the edge, such as the NordWestZentrum (3,000 spaces at €1 an hour), offer a cheap alternative to the centre.

sections.title: Operators, location, price and use
sections.text:
PBG dominates the centre: 63% of its spaces are within a kilometre of the Hauptwache. It prices about 8% below its neighbours (typically €2 an hour, €32 a day), and its garages are the busiest we measure, 55% on weekdays, with the Hauptwache garage at 74%. APCOA is as large but sits mostly outside the centre, at hospitals, offices and the airport business park, at about €2.30 an hour and 34% occupied. Q-Park's seven sites include the NordWestZentrum; we do not measure them. Contipark is the price outlier, about 40% above its neighbours, including near the station.

Centre garages are well used (51–54% within a kilometre), the ring one to two kilometres out, which takes in the area around the Messe, is much quieter (36%) and dearer (typically €3), and the emptiest garages are the most expensive ones, Messeturm and Mövenpick at €5 an hour (7–18%). The fullest site in the city is a park-and-ride, Borsigallee (80%).
